`tmp_path` is pytest's equivalent of JUnit 5's `@TempDir`: a fresh, empty directory created for each individual test function, handed to you as a `pathlib.Path`.

## How the injection works

Python has no annotations here — pytest matches **by parameter name**. When it sees `def test_compresses_old_logs(tmp_path)`, it looks up a registered fixture called `tmp_path`, calls it, and passes the result as that argument. It's dependency injection where the parameter name is the bean name. `tmp_path` is built into pytest, so nothing has to be imported or declared.

You define your own fixtures with the `@pytest.fixture` decorator (in the test file or in a shared `conftest.py`, which acts like an implicit base class / auto-discovered config for the whole directory tree). Note that `make()` at line 6 is *not* a fixture — it's a plain helper that the tests call explicitly, which is why `tmp_path` has to be passed into it manually.

## What tmp_path actually gives you

- A unique path like `/tmp/pytest-of-your-username/pytest-31/test_compresses_old_logs0`, already created.
- Scope is **per test function**. Each of the three tests in this file gets its own directory, even though all three create a file named `a.log`.
- No teardown code. pytest retains the last 3 runs' directories (handy for post-mortem debugging of a failure) and deletes older ones automatically.
- It's a `Path`, not a string — hence `tmp_path / name` (line 7), where `/` is overloaded for path joining, roughly `Path.of(dir).resolve(name)`.
- If you need one shared across a whole test session, that's a different fixture, `tmp_path_factory`.

## Why this suite needs it

Three reasons specific to `rotate_logs.py`:

**It deletes files.** `compress()` calls `path.unlink()` (line 23) and `prune_archives()` unlinks every archive beyond the newest `keep` (line 30). Pointing tests at a fixed directory means a bug — or just running the suite from the wrong working directory — permanently destroys whatever was in it. A throwaway directory makes destructive behavior safe to exercise.

**The assertions depend on the directory being exactly what the test created.** `test_prunes_to_keep` asserts `len(list(tmp_path.glob("*.gz"))) == 2`. In a fixed directory, one leftover `.gz` from a previous run makes that 3 and the test fails — and it would fail *only on the second run*, the worst kind of flake. Same for `test_compresses_old_logs`, which asserts the rotated list is exactly `["a.log.gz"]`.

**The tests mutate filesystem metadata.** `make()` backdates mtime with `os.utime` (line 10) so `is_older_than` sees a 10-day-old file without waiting 10 days. That's a real side effect on a real file; you want it confined to a directory nobody else owns.

The isolation also means the suite is safe to run in parallel (e.g. `pytest -n auto` with pytest-xdist) and doesn't need `try/finally` cleanup — the Java habit of writing an `@AfterEach` to `deleteRecursively` the directory is simply absent, because the fixture owns that lifecycle.
